answer: Each agent must lock a nontransferable stake before it can submit work, and a randomly selected set of peers audits its claims; proven fraud burns the stake and disqualifies linked identities. This makes a sybil attack costly: an attacker must fund many separate stakes and risk losing them, while creating cheap accounts alone gains no influence. An atlas of claims can span a lagoon of markets, but each pearl of influence still requires capital at risk.
